source: Following al-Farabi's lead, Avicenna initiated a full-fledged inquiry into the question of being, in which he distinguished between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud). He argued that the fact of existence can not be inferred from or accounted for by the essence of existing things, and that form and matter by themselves cannot interact and originate the movement of the universe or the progressive actualization of existing things. Existence must, therefore, be due to an agent-cause that necessitates, imparts, gives, or adds existence to an essence. To do so, the cause must be an existing thing and coexist with its effect.
output: Inspired by al-Farabi, Avicenna conducted a comprehensive investigation into the nature of being, establishing a distinction between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud). He contended that existence cannot be derived from or explained by the essence of an object, nor can the interaction of form and matter alone account for cosmic movement or the actualization of entities. Consequently, he argued that existence must originate from an agent-cause that bestows it upon an essence. This cause must be an existing entity that coexists simultaneously with its effect.

source: In winter, the Piedmont is colder than the coast, with temperatures usually averaging in the upper 40s–lower 50s °F (8–12 °C) during the day and often dropping below the freezing point at night. The region averages around 3–5 in (8–13 cm) of snowfall annually in the Charlotte area, and slightly more north toward the Virginia border. The Piedmont is especially notorious for sleet and freezing rain. Freezing rain can be heavy enough to snarl traffic and break down trees and power lines. Annual precipitation and humidity are lower in the Piedmont than in the mountains or the coast, but even at its lowest, the average is 40 in (1,020 mm) per year.

source: After a decade of constant warfare, France and Britain signed the Treaty of Amiens in March 1802, bringing the Revolutionary Wars to an end. Amiens called for the withdrawal of British troops from recently conquered colonial territories as well as for assurances to curtail the expansionary goals of the French Republic. With Europe at peace and the economy recovering, Napoleon's popularity soared to its highest levels under the Consulate, both domestically and abroad. In a new plebiscite during the spring of 1802, the French public came out in huge numbers to approve a constitution that made the Consulate permanent, essentially elevating Napoleon to dictator for life. Whereas the plebiscite two years earlier had brought out 1.5 million people to the polls, the new referendum enticed 3.6 million to go and vote (72% of all eligible voters). There was no secret ballot in 1802 and few people wanted to openly defy the regime; the constitution gained approval with over 99% of the vote. His broad powers were spelled out in the new constitution: Article 1. The French people name, and the Senate proclaims Napoleon-Bonaparte First Consul for Life. After 1802, he was generally referred to as Napoleon rather than Bonaparte.
output: The Treaty of Amiens, signed in March 1802, concluded a decade of continuous conflict between France and Britain. The agreement required Britain to withdraw troops from conquered colonies and demanded that the French Republic limit its expansionist ambitions. This period of peace and economic recovery propelled Napoleon to unprecedented levels of popularity both at home and abroad. In the spring of 1802, a massive plebiscite saw 3.6 million people—72% of eligible voters—turn out to approve a new constitution. This document made the Consulate permanent, effectively establishing Napoleon as a dictator for life. Because there was no secret ballot and public dissent was rare, the constitution received over 99% approval. The new constitution explicitly granted him broad authority, with Article 1 naming him "First Consul for Life." Following 1802, he was commonly known simply as Napoleon rather than Napoleon Bonaparte.

source: From the 17th through 19th centuries, the merging of folk beliefs about group differences with scientific explanations of those differences produced what one scholar has called an "ideology of race". According to this ideology, races are primordial, natural, enduring and distinct. It was further argued that some groups may be the result of mixture between formerly distinct populations, but that careful study could distinguish the ancestral races that had combined to produce admixed groups. Subsequent influential classifications by Georges Buffon, Petrus Camper and Christoph Meiners all classified "Negros" as inferior to Europeans. In the United States the racial theories of Thomas Jefferson were influential. He saw Africans as inferior to Whites especially in regards to their intellect, and imbued with unnatural sexual appetites, but described Native Americans as equals to whites.
output: Between the 17th and 19th centuries, the synthesis of folk beliefs regarding group differences and scientific inquiry gave rise to an "ideology of race." This framework posited that races were natural, enduring, and distinct biological entities. While proponents acknowledged that some groups resulted from the mixing of populations, they maintained that scientific analysis could isolate the original ancestral lineages within admixed groups. Influential classifications by figures such as Georges Buffon, Petrus Camper, and Christoph Meiners categorized "Negros" as inferior to Europeans. In the United States, Thomas Jefferson’s racial theories were highly influential; he characterized Africans as intellectually inferior and driven by unnatural sexual desires, while conversely viewing Native Americans as equals to whites.

source: Czech distinguishes three genders—masculine, feminine, and neuter—and the masculine gender is subdivided into animate and inanimate. With few exceptions, feminine nouns in the nominative case end in -a, -e, or -ost; neuter nouns in -o, -e, or -í, and masculine nouns in a consonant. Adjectives agree in gender and animacy (for masculine nouns in the accusative or genitive singular and the nominative plural) with the nouns they modify. The main effect of gender in Czech is the difference in noun and adjective declension, but other effects include past-tense verb endings: for example, dělal (he did, or made); dělala (she did, or made) and dělalo (it did, or made).
output: Czech features three genders—masculine, feminine, and neuter—with the masculine category further divided into animate and inanimate. Generally, feminine nouns in the nominative case end in -a, -e, or -ost; neuter nouns end in -o, -e, or -í; and masculine nouns typically end in a consonant. Adjectives must agree with the gender and animacy of the nouns they modify, particularly in the masculine accusative and genitive singular, as well as the nominative plural. While gender primarily influences noun and adjective declension, it also affects past-tense verb endings, such as dělal (masculine), dělala (feminine), and dělalo (neuter).

source: The native language of Germans is German, a West Germanic language, related to and classified alongside English and Dutch, and sharing many similarities with the North Germanic and Scandinavian languages. Spoken by approximately 100 million native speakers, German is one of the world's major languages and the most widely spoken first language in the European Union. German has been replaced by English as the dominant language of science-related Nobel Prize laureates during the second half of the 20th century. It was a lingua franca in the Holy Roman Empire.

source: The most innovative period of Cubism was before 1914. After World War I, with the support given by the dealer Léonce Rosenberg, Cubism returned as a central issue for artists, and continued as such until the mid-1920s when its avant-garde status was rendered questionable by the emergence of geometric abstraction and Surrealism in Paris. Many Cubists, including Picasso, Braque, Gris, Léger, Gleizes, and Metzinger, while developing other styles, returned periodically to Cubism, even well after 1925. Cubism reemerged during the 1920s and the 1930s in the work of the American Stuart Davis and the Englishman Ben Nicholson. In France, however, Cubism experienced a decline beginning in about 1925. Léonce Rosenberg exhibited not only the artists stranded by Kahnweiler’s exile but others including Laurens, Lipchitz, Metzinger, Gleizes, Csaky, Herbin and Severini. In 1918 Rosenberg presented a series of Cubist exhibitions at his Galerie de l’Effort Moderne in Paris. Attempts were made by Louis Vauxcelles to claim that Cubism was dead, but these exhibitions, along with a well-organized Cubist show at the 1920 Salon des Indépendants and a revival of the Salon de la Section d’Or in the same year, demonstrated it was still alive.
output: Cubism reached its peak of innovation prior to 1914. Following World War I, the movement regained prominence as a primary focus for artists, bolstered by the support of dealer Léonce Rosenberg. This continued until the mid-1920s, when the rise of Surrealism and geometric abstraction in Paris began to challenge its avant-garde status. Despite this shift, many prominent Cubists—such as Picasso, Braque, Gris, Léger, Gleizes, and Metzinger—periodically returned to the style even after 1925 while exploring other aesthetics. During the 1920s and 1930s, Cubism saw a resurgence in the works of Ben Nicholson and Stuart Davis, though it began to wane in France around 1925. During this period, Rosenberg exhibited a diverse group of artists, including Laurens, Lipchitz, Metzinger, Gleizes, Csaky, Herbin, and Severini. Although Louis Vauxcelles attempted to declare the movement dead, a series of exhibitions by Rosenberg in 1918, a major show at the 1920 Salon des Indépendants, and the revival of the Salon de la Section d’Or that same year proved that Cubism remained a vital force.

source: German historian Reinhart Koselleck claimed that "On the Continent there were two social structures that left a decisive imprint on the Age of Enlightenment: the Republic of Letters and the Masonic lodges." Scottish professor Thomas Munck argues that "although the Masons did promote international and cross-social contacts which were essentially non-religious and broadly in agreement with enlightened values, they can hardly be described as a major radical or reformist network in their own right." Many of the Masons values seemed to greatly appeal to Enlightenment values and thinkers. Diderot discusses the link between Freemason ideals and the enlightenment in D'Alembert's Dream, exploring masonry as a way of spreading enlightenment beliefs. Historian Margaret Jacob stresses the importance of the Masons in indirectly inspiring enlightened political thought. On the negative side, Daniel Roche contests claims that Masonry promoted egalitarianism. He argues that the lodges only attracted men of similar social backgrounds. The presence of noble women in the French "lodges of adoption" that formed in the 1780s was largely due to the close ties shared between these lodges and aristocratic society.
output: German historian Reinhart Koselleck identified the Republic of Letters and Masonic lodges as two pivotal social structures that shaped the Age of Enlightenment. While Scottish professor Thomas Munck acknowledges that Freemasonry fostered international, non-religious connections aligned with enlightened ideals, he contends that the organization was not a primary radical or reformist network. Nevertheless, Masonic values resonated deeply with Enlightenment thinkers; for instance, Diderot’s *D'Alembert's Dream* explores masonry as a vehicle for disseminating these beliefs, and historian Margaret Jacob highlights the Masons' role in indirectly inspiring enlightened political theory. Conversely, Daniel Roche challenges the notion that Masonry promoted egalitarianism, arguing that lodges primarily attracted men from similar social strata. He suggests that the inclusion of noblewomen in the French "lodges of adoption" during the 1780s was a result of the organization's close ties to the aristocracy rather than a move toward social equality.

Nevertheless, Masonic values resonated deeply with Enlightenment thinkers; for instance, Diderot’s *D'Alembert's Dream* explores masonry as a vehicle for disseminating these beliefs, and historian Margaret Jacob highlights the Masons' role in indirectly inspiring enlightened political theory. Conversely, Daniel Roche challenges the notion that Masonry promoted egalitarianism, arguing that lodges primarily attracted men from similar social strata. He suggests that the inclusion of noblewomen in the French "lodges of adoption" during the 1780s was a result of the organization's close ties to the aristocracy rather than a move toward social equality.

source: In response to a given problem situation (), a number of competing conjectures, or tentative theories (), are systematically subjected to the most rigorous attempts at falsification possible. This process, error elimination (), performs a similar function for science that natural selection performs for biological evolution. Theories that better survive the process of refutation are not more true, but rather, more "fit"—in other words, more applicable to the problem situation at hand (). Consequently, just as a species' biological fitness does not ensure continued survival, neither does rigorous testing protect a scientific theory from refutation in the future. Yet, as it appears that the engine of biological evolution has, over many generations, produced adaptive traits equipped to deal with more and more complex problems of survival, likewise, the evolution of theories through the scientific method may, in Popper's view, reflect a certain type of progress: toward more and more interesting problems (). For Popper, it is in the interplay between the tentative theories (conjectures) and error elimination (refutation) that scientific knowledge advances toward greater and greater problems; in a process very much akin to the interplay between genetic variation and natural selection.

Just as biological fitness does not guarantee a species' eternal survival, rigorous testing does not shield a scientific theory from future refutation. However, just as biological evolution produces increasingly adaptive traits for complex survival challenges, Popper argues that the evolution of theories through the scientific method represents a form of progress toward more complex problems. For Popper, scientific knowledge advances through the interplay between conjectures and refutation in a manner strikingly similar to the interplay between genetic variation and natural selection.

source: and Camargo. In 1631 Juan Rangel de Biezma discovered a rich vein of silver, and subsequently established San Jose del Parral near the site. Parral remained an important economic and cultural center for the next 300 years. On December 8, 1659 Fray García de San Francisco founded the mission of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe de Mansos del Paso del Río del Norte and founded the town El Paso Del Norte (present day Ciudad Juárez) in 1667. The Spanish society that developed in the region replaced the sparse population of indigenous peoples. The absence of servants and workers forged the spirit of northern people as self-dependent, creative people that defended their European heritage. In 1680 settlers from Santa Fe, New Mexico sought refuge in El Paso Del Norte for twelve years after fleeing the attacks from Pueblo tribes, but returned to Santa Fe in 1692 after Diego de Vargas recaptured the city and vicinity. In 1709, Antonio de Deza y Ulloa founded the state capital Chihuahua City; shortly after, the city became the headquarters for the regional mining offices of the Spanish crown known as Real de Minas de San Francisco de Cuéllar in honor of the Viceroy of New Spain, Francisco Fernández de la Cueva Enríquez, Duke of Alburquerque and the Marquee of Cuéllar..

source: As the premiers did not come to an agreement on this question, the Parliamentary Council was supposed to address this issue. Its provisions are reflected in Article 29. There was a binding provision for a new delimitation of the federal territory: the Federal Territory must be revised ... (paragraph 1). Moreover, in territories or parts of territories whose affiliation with a Land had changed after 8 May 1945 without a referendum, people were allowed to petition for a revision of the current status within a year after the promulgation of the Basic Law (paragraph 2). If at least one tenth of those entitled to vote in Bundestag elections were in favour of a revision, the federal government had to include the proposal into its legislation. Then a referendum was required in each territory or part of a territory whose affiliation was to be changed (paragraph 3). The proposal should not take effect if within any of the affected territories a majority rejected the change. In this case, the bill had to be introduced again and after passing had to be confirmed by referendum in the Federal Republic as a whole (paragraph 4). The reorganization should be completed within three years after the Basic Law had come into force (paragraph 6).
output: Because the premiers failed to reach an agreement on this matter, the Parliamentary Council was tasked with addressing it, resulting in the provisions of Article 29. This article included a binding mandate to revise the delimitation of the federal territory (paragraph 1). Additionally, residents of territories or parts of territories whose affiliation with a Land had changed after May 8, 1945, without a referendum, were permitted to petition for a status revision within one year of the Basic Law's promulgation (paragraph 2). If at least one-tenth of the eligible voters for Bundestag elections supported the revision, the federal government was required to incorporate the proposal into legislation (paragraph 3). Subsequently, a referendum was required in each affected territory or part of a territory. The proposal would fail if a majority in any of the affected areas rejected the change; in such instances, the bill had to be reintroduced and, upon passing, confirmed by a nationwide referendum in the Federal Republic (paragraph 4). The reorganization was to be finalized within three years of the Basic Law taking effect (paragraph 6).

source: Santa Bárbara became the launching place for expeditions into New Mexico by Spanish conquistadors like: Antonio de Espejo, Gaspar Castaño, Antonio Gutiérrez de Umaña, Francisco Leyba de Bonilla, and Vicente de Zaldívar. Several expeditions were led to find a shorter route from Santa Barbara to New Mexico. In April 1598, Juan de Oñate finally found a short route from Santa Barbara to New Mexico which came to be called El Paso del Norte (The Northern Pass). The discovery of El Paso Del Norte was important for the expansion of El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro (The Inner Land Royal Road) to link Spanish settlements in New Mexico to Mexico City; El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro facilitated transport of settlers and supplies to New Mexico.
output: Santa Bárbara served as the starting point for several Spanish conquistador expeditions into New Mexico, including those led by Antonio de Espejo, Gaspar Castaño, Antonio Gutiérrez de Umaña, Francisco Leyba de Bonilla, and Vicente de Zaldívar. These missions sought a more direct path to the territory, eventually leading Juan de Oñate to discover a shorter route in April 1598 known as El Paso del Norte (The Northern Pass). This discovery was crucial for the expansion of El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro (The Inner Land Royal Road), which connected Spanish settlements in New Mexico to Mexico City and provided a vital corridor for transporting settlers and supplies.

source: As explained by Richard Meade in the English Journal of the (American) National Council of Teachers of English, the form daylight savings time (with an "s") was already in 1978 much more common than the older form daylight saving time in American English ("the change has been virtually accomplished"). Nevertheless, even dictionaries such as Merriam-Webster's, American Heritage, and Oxford, which describe actual usage instead of prescribing outdated usage (and therefore also list the newer form), still list the older form first. This is because the older form is still very common in print and preferred by many editors. ("Although daylight saving time is considered correct, daylight savings time (with an "s") is commonly used.") The first two words are sometimes hyphenated (daylight-saving[s] time). Merriam-Webster's also lists the forms daylight saving (without "time"), daylight savings (without "time"), and daylight time.
output: Richard Meade, writing in the *English Journal of the (American) National Council of Teachers of English*, noted that by 1978, "daylight savings time" had become significantly more prevalent in American English than the traditional "daylight saving time." Despite this shift in common usage, major dictionaries like Merriam-Webster, American Heritage, and Oxford still prioritize the older form. While these publications acknowledge that "daylight savings time" is widely used, they maintain the original phrasing as the primary entry because it remains common in print and is preferred by many editors. Additionally, the first two words are occasionally hyphenated as "daylight-saving[s] time," and Merriam-Webster also recognizes variations such as "daylight saving," "daylight savings," and "daylight time."

source: Israel has two official languages, Hebrew and Arabic. Hebrew is the primary language of the state and is spoken everyday by the majority of the population, and Arabic is spoken by the Arab minority and Hebrew is taught in Arab schools. English was an official language during the Mandate period; it lost this status after the creation of Israel, but retains a role comparable to that of an official language, as may be seen in road signs and official documents. Many Israelis communicate reasonably well in English, as many television programs are broadcast in English with subtitles and the language is taught from the early grades in elementary school. In addition, Israeli universities offer courses in the English language on various subjects. As a country of immigrants, many languages can be heard on the streets. Due to mass immigration from the former Soviet Union and Ethiopia (some 130,000 Ethiopian Jews live in Israel), Russian and Amharic are widely spoken. More than one million Russian-speaking immigrants arrived in Israel from the former Soviet Union states between 1990 and 2004. French is spoken by around 700,000 Israelis, mostly originating from France and North Africa (see Maghrebi Jews).
output: Israel recognizes Hebrew and Arabic as its two official languages. Hebrew serves as the primary language for the majority of the population, while Arabic is spoken by the Arab minority; notably, Hebrew is also taught in Arab schools. Although English lost its official status following the establishment of Israel, it remains highly prevalent in official documentation and road signage. English proficiency is widespread due to its inclusion in the elementary school curriculum, its use in subtitled television programming, and its role as a medium of instruction for various university courses. Furthermore, Israel's history as a nation of immigrants has resulted in a diverse linguistic landscape. Russian and Amharic are common due to significant migration from the former Soviet Union and Ethiopia, with over one million Russian speakers arriving between 1990 and 2004. Additionally, approximately 700,000 Israelis speak French, primarily those of French and North African descent.

source: In 1982, the US Mint began minting pennies coated in copper but made primarily of zinc. With the new zinc pennies, there is the potential for zinc toxicosis, which can be fatal. One reported case of chronic ingestion of 425 pennies (over 1 kg of zinc) resulted in death due to gastrointestinal bacterial and fungal sepsis, whereas another patient, who ingested 12 grams of zinc, only showed lethargy and ataxia (gross lack of coordination of muscle movements). Several other cases have been reported of humans suffering zinc intoxication by the ingestion of zinc coins.
output: Starting in 1982, the US Mint produced pennies primarily composed of zinc with a copper coating. These coins pose a risk of zinc toxicosis, a potentially fatal condition. Reported cases of zinc coin ingestion vary in severity: one individual died from gastrointestinal bacterial and fungal sepsis after consuming 425 pennies (over 1 kg of zinc), while another patient who ingested 12 grams of zinc experienced only lethargy and ataxia. Numerous other instances of human zinc intoxication from coin ingestion have been documented.

source: The entire Protestant canon of scripture is considered the inspired, inerrant word of God. Jehovah's Witnesses consider the Bible to be scientifically and historically accurate and reliable and interpret much of it literally, but accept parts of it as symbolic. They consider the Bible to be the final authority for all their beliefs, although sociologist Andrew Holden's ethnographic study of the religion concluded that pronouncements of the Governing Body, through Watch Tower Society publications, carry almost as much weight as the Bible. Regular personal Bible reading is frequently recommended; Witnesses are discouraged from formulating doctrines and "private ideas" reached through Bible research independent of Watch Tower Society publications, and are cautioned against reading other religious literature. Adherents are told to have "complete confidence" in the leadership, avoid skepticism about what is taught in the Watch Tower Society's literature, and "not advocate or insist on personal opinions or harbor private ideas when it comes to Bible understanding." The religion makes no provision for members to criticize or contribute to official teachings and all Witnesses must abide by its doctrines and organizational requirements.

source: The Laurentian Highlands, the Interior Plains and the Interior Highlands lie between the two coasts, stretching from the Gulf of Mexico northward, far beyond the national boundary, to the Arctic Ocean. The central plains are divided by a hardly perceptible height of land into a Canadian and a United States portion. It is from the United States side, that the great Mississippi system discharges southward to the Gulf of Mexico. The upper Mississippi and some of the Ohio basin is the semi-arid prairie region, with trees originally only along the watercourses. The uplands towards the Appalachians were included in the great eastern forested area, while the western part of the plains has so dry a climate that its native plant life is scanty, and in the south it is practically barren.
output: Stretching from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean, the Laurentian Highlands, Interior Plains, and Interior Highlands span the land between the two coasts. A subtle height of land divides the central plains into Canadian and United States territories, with the Mississippi system flowing southward into the Gulf from the American side. The upper Mississippi and parts of the Ohio basin comprise a semi-arid prairie where trees were originally confined to waterways. In contrast, the uplands near the Appalachians were part of a vast eastern forest, while the western plains feature a much drier climate with sparse native vegetation that becomes nearly barren in the south.

source: Anthropologists have contributed to the debate by shifting the focus of research: One of the first challenges for the researcher wishing to carry out empirical research in this area is to identify an appropriate analytical tool. The concept of boundaries is useful here for demonstrating how identity works. In the same way as Barth, in his approach to ethnicity, advocated the critical focus for investigation as being "the ethnic boundary that defines the group rather than the cultural stuff that it encloses" (1969:15), social anthropologists such as Cohen and Bray have shifted the focus of analytical study from identity to the boundaries that are used for purposes of identification. If identity is a kind of virtual site in which the dynamic processes and markers used for identification are made apparent, boundaries provide the framework on which this virtual site is built. They concentrated on how the idea of community belonging is differently constructed by individual members and how individuals within the group conceive ethnic boundaries.
output: Anthropologists have shaped the debate by redirecting research toward the mechanisms of identification. A primary challenge for empirical researchers in this field is selecting an appropriate analytical framework, where the concept of "boundaries" serves as a vital tool for understanding identity. Mirroring Fredrik Barth’s assertion that ethnicity is defined by the boundaries between groups rather than the internal cultural content (1969:15), social anthropologists like Cohen and Bray have shifted the analytical focus from identity itself to the boundaries used to establish it. In this view, if identity is a virtual space where the processes of identification become visible, boundaries constitute the underlying framework of that space. Consequently, research has centered on how individual members construct their sense of community belonging and how they perceive the ethnic boundaries that define their group.

source: The key characteristic of classical music that distinguishes it from popular music and folk music is that the repertoire tends to be written down in musical notation, creating a musical part or score. This score typically determines details of rhythm, pitch, and, where two or more musicians (whether singers or instrumentalists) are involved, how the various parts are coordinated. The written quality of the music has enabled a high level of complexity within them: J.S. Bach's fugues, for instance, achieve a remarkable marriage of boldly distinctive melodic lines weaving in counterpoint yet creating a coherent harmonic logic that would be impossible in the heat of live improvisation. The use of written notation also preserves a record of the works and enables Classical musicians to perform music from many centuries ago. Musical notation enables 2000s-era performers to sing a choral work from the 1300s Renaissance era or a 1700s Baroque concerto with many of the features of the music (the melodies, lyrics, forms, and rhythms) being reproduced.
output: Unlike popular and folk music, classical music is primarily defined by its reliance on written notation. These scores dictate specific details regarding rhythm, pitch, and the coordination of multiple performers. This written format allows for a level of complexity—such as the intricate counterpoint and harmonic logic found in J.S. Bach's fugues—that would be difficult to achieve through live improvisation alone. Furthermore, notation serves as a historical record, allowing modern musicians to accurately reproduce the melodies, lyrics, forms, and rhythms of works spanning centuries, from the 1300s Renaissance to the 1700s Baroque era.

source: The Maurya Empire (322–185 BCE) was the first empire to unify India into one state, and was the largest on the Indian subcontinent. At its greatest extent, the Mauryan Empire stretched to the north up to the natural boundaries of the Himalayas and to the east into what is now Assam. To the west, it reached beyond modern Pakistan, to the Hindu Kush mountains in what is now Afghanistan. The empire was established by Chandragupta Maurya in Magadha (in modern Bihar) when he overthrew the Nanda Dynasty. Chandragupta's son Bindusara succeeded to the throne around 297 BC. By the time he died in c. 272 BC, a large part of the subcontinent was under Mauryan suzerainty. However, the region of Kalinga (around modern day Odisha) remained outside Mauryan control, perhaps interfering with their trade with the south.

At its peak, the empire's territory extended from the Himalayas in the north to modern-day Assam in the east, and beyond modern Pakistan to the Hindu Kush mountains in the west. Chandragupta's successor, Bindusara, inherited the throne around 297 BC and expanded the empire's reach significantly by 272 BC. Despite this vast expansion, the region of Kalinga (near modern Odisha) remained independent, potentially obstructing Mauryan trade routes to the south.

source: Tennessee was admitted to the Union on June 1, 1796 as the 16th state. It was the first state created from territory under the jurisdiction of the United States federal government. Apart from the former Thirteen Colonies only Vermont and Kentucky predate Tennessee's statehood, and neither was ever a federal territory. The state boundaries, according to the Constitution of the State of Tennessee, Article I, Section 31, stated that the beginning point for identifying the boundary was the extreme height of the Stone Mountain, at the place where the line of Virginia intersects it, and basically ran the extreme heights of mountain chains through the Appalachian Mountains separating North Carolina from Tennessee past the Indian towns of Cowee and Old Chota, thence along the main ridge of the said mountain (Unicoi Mountain) to the southern boundary of the state; all the territory, lands and waters lying west of said line are included in the boundaries and limits of the newly formed state of Tennessee. Part of the provision also stated that the limits and jurisdiction of the state would include future land acquisition, referencing possible land trade with other states, or the acquisition of territory from west of the Mississippi River.
output: Tennessee became the 16th state admitted to the Union on June 1, 1796. It holds the distinction of being the first state established from territory under federal jurisdiction; notably, only Vermont and Kentucky were admitted before it, and neither originated as a federal territory. According to Article I, Section 31 of the State Constitution, the state's boundaries were defined starting from the peak of Stone Mountain at the Virginia border. The line followed the Appalachian mountain chains separating North Carolina and Tennessee, passing the Indian towns of Cowee and Old Chota, and continuing along the main ridge of Unicoi Mountain to the southern border. All lands and waters west of this line were included in the state. Additionally, the provision stipulated that the state's jurisdiction would encompass any future land acquisitions, including potential trades with other states or territories gained west of the Mississippi River.

source: In the 7th century, the Frankish merchant Samo, who supported the Slavs fighting their Avar rulers, became the ruler of the first known Slav state in Central Europe, which, however, most probably did not outlive its founder and ruler. This provided the foundation for subsequent Slavic states to arise on the former territory of this realm with Carantania being the oldest of them. Very old also are the Principality of Nitra and the Moravian principality (see under Great Moravia). In this period, there existed central Slavic groups and states such as the Balaton Principality, but the subsequent expansion of the Magyars, as well as the Germanisation of Austria, separated the northern and southern Slavs. The First Bulgarian Empire was founded in 681, the Slavic language Old Bulgarian became the main and official of the empire in 864. Bulgaria was instrumental in the spread of Slavic literacy and Christianity to the rest of the Slavic world.
output: During the 7th century, the Frankish merchant Samo established the first known Slavic state in Central Europe after supporting the Slavs against Avar rule. Although this state likely collapsed shortly after his death, it laid the groundwork for future Slavic entities, including Carantania, the Principality of Nitra, and the Moravian principality. While central Slavic groups like the Balaton Principality existed during this era, the later expansion of the Magyars and the Germanization of Austria eventually divided the Slavic populations into northern and southern groups. Meanwhile, the First Bulgarian Empire was founded in 681, adopting Old Bulgarian as its official language in 864. Bulgaria played a pivotal role in disseminating Christianity and Slavic literacy throughout the Slavic world.

source: Ann Arbor was founded in 1824 by land speculators John Allen and Elisha Walker Rumsey. On 25 May 1824, the town plat was registered with Wayne County as "Annarbour;" this represents the earliest known use of the town's name. Allen and Rumsey decided to name it for their wives, both named Ann, and for the stands of Bur Oak in the 640 acres (260 ha) of land they purchased for $800 from the federal government at $1.25 per acre. The local Ojibwa named the settlement kaw-goosh-kaw-nick, after the sound of Allen's sawmill.

source: Following al-Farabi's lead, Avicenna initiated a full-fledged inquiry into the question of being, in which he distinguished between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud). He argued that the fact of existence can not be inferred from or accounted for by the essence of existing things, and that form and matter by themselves cannot interact and originate the movement of the universe or the progressive actualization of existing things. Existence must, therefore, be due to an agent-cause that necessitates, imparts, gives, or adds existence to an essence. To do so, the cause must be an existing thing and coexist with its effect.

Avicenna argued that existence cannot be explained by essence. He stated that form and matter cannot interact to create movement or cause things to change. Existence must come from an agent-cause. This cause must be an existing thing. It must coexist with the thing it gives existence to.

source: Czech distinguishes three genders—masculine, feminine, and neuter—and the masculine gender is subdivided into animate and inanimate. With few exceptions, feminine nouns in the nominative case end in -a, -e, or -ost; neuter nouns in -o, -e, or -í, and masculine nouns in a consonant. Adjectives agree in gender and animacy (for masculine nouns in the accusative or genitive singular and the nominative plural) with the nouns they modify. The main effect of gender in Czech is the difference in noun and adjective declension, but other effects include past-tense verb endings: for example, dělal (he did, or made); dělala (she did, or made) and dělalo (it did, or made).

source: In response to a given problem situation (), a number of competing conjectures, or tentative theories (), are systematically subjected to the most rigorous attempts at falsification possible. This process, error elimination (), performs a similar function for science that natural selection performs for biological evolution. Theories that better survive the process of refutation are not more true, but rather, more "fit"—in other words, more applicable to the problem situation at hand (). Consequently, just as a species' biological fitness does not ensure continued survival, neither does rigorous testing protect a scientific theory from refutation in the future. Yet, as it appears that the engine of biological evolution has, over many generations, produced adaptive traits equipped to deal with more and more complex problems of survival, likewise, the evolution of theories through the scientific method may, in Popper's view, reflect a certain type of progress: toward more and more interesting problems (). For Popper, it is in the interplay between the tentative theories (conjectures) and error elimination (refutation) that scientific knowledge advances toward greater and greater problems; in a process very much akin to the interplay between genetic variation and natural selection.

However, biological evolution produces adaptive traits over time. Similarly, the scientific method produces progress. Scientific knowledge advances through the interplay of conjectures and refutation. This process is similar to the interplay between genetic variation and natural selection.

source: As the premiers did not come to an agreement on this question, the Parliamentary Council was supposed to address this issue. Its provisions are reflected in Article 29. There was a binding provision for a new delimitation of the federal territory: the Federal Territory must be revised ... (paragraph 1). Moreover, in territories or parts of territories whose affiliation with a Land had changed after 8 May 1945 without a referendum, people were allowed to petition for a revision of the current status within a year after the promulgation of the Basic Law (paragraph 2). If at least one tenth of those entitled to vote in Bundestag elections were in favour of a revision, the federal government had to include the proposal into its legislation. Then a referendum was required in each territory or part of a territory whose affiliation was to be changed (paragraph 3). The proposal should not take effect if within any of the affected territories a majority rejected the change. In this case, the bill had to be introduced again and after passing had to be confirmed by referendum in the Federal Republic as a whole (paragraph 4). The reorganization should be completed within three years after the Basic Law had come into force (paragraph 6).

If at least one-tenth of the voters supported the revision, the federal government had to include it in a bill. A referendum was required for each affected territory. The proposal would fail if any affected territory rejected it. If it was rejected, the bill had to be reintroduced and confirmed by a national referendum. source: Anthropologists have contributed to the debate by shifting the focus of research: One of the first challenges for the researcher wishing to carry out empirical research in this area is to identify an appropriate analytical tool. The concept of boundaries is useful here for demonstrating how identity works. In the same way as Barth, in his approach to ethnicity, advocated the critical focus for investigation as being "the ethnic boundary that defines the group rather than the cultural stuff that it encloses" (1969:15), social anthropologists such as Cohen and Bray have shifted the focus of analytical study from identity to the boundaries that are used for purposes of identification. If identity is a kind of virtual site in which the dynamic processes and markers used for identification are made apparent, boundaries provide the framework on which this virtual site is built. They concentrated on how the idea of community belonging is differently constructed by individual members and how individuals within the group conceive ethnic boundaries.

Following Fredrik Barth’s approach, which prioritizes ethnic boundaries over cultural content, social anthropologists like Cohen and Bray focus on the boundaries used for identification. They focus on how members perceive and conceive of ethnic boundaries.

baseline_output: Anthropologists have shaped the debate by redirecting research toward the mechanisms of identification. A primary challenge for empirical researchers in this field is selecting an appropriate analytical framework, where the concept of "boundaries" serves as a vital tool for understanding identity. Mirroring Fredrik Barth’s assertion that ethnicity is defined by the boundaries between groups rather than the internal cultural content (1969:15), social anthropologists like Cohen and Bray have shifted the analytical focus from identity itself to the boundaries used to establish it. In this view, if identity is a virtual space where the processes of identification become visible, boundaries constitute the underlying framework of that space. Consequently, research has centered on how individual members construct their sense of community belonging and how they perceive the ethnic boundaries that define their group.

source: The key characteristic of classical music that distinguishes it from popular music and folk music is that the repertoire tends to be written down in musical notation, creating a musical part or score. This score typically determines details of rhythm, pitch, and, where two or more musicians (whether singers or instrumentalists) are involved, how the various parts are coordinated. The written quality of the music has enabled a high level of complexity within them: J.S. Bach's fugues, for instance, achieve a remarkable marriage of boldly distinctive melodic lines weaving in counterpoint yet creating a coherent harmonic logic that would be impossible in the heat of live improvisation. The use of written notation also preserves a record of the works and enables Classical musicians to perform music from many centuries ago. Musical notation enables 2000s-era performers to sing a choral work from the 1300s Renaissance era or a 1700s Baroque concerto with many of the features of the music (the melodies, lyrics, forms, and rhythms) being reproduced.
output: Unlike popular and folk music, classical music is defined by its use of musical notation. These scores specify the rhythm, pitch, and coordination between performers. Written notation allows for high levels of complexity. For example, J.S. Bach’s fugues feature complex counterpoint and harmonic logic that are difficult to achieve through improvisation. Notation also preserves music over time. It allows modern performers to play works from the Renaissance and Baroque periods while preserving their original melodies, lyrics, and forms.

These scores dictate specific details regarding rhythm, pitch, and the coordination of multiple performers. This written format allows for a level of complexity—such as the intricate counterpoint and harmonic logic found in J.S. Bach's fugues—that would be difficult to achieve through live improvisation alone. source: The Maurya Empire (322–185 BCE) was the first empire to unify India into one state, and was the largest on the Indian subcontinent. At its greatest extent, the Mauryan Empire stretched to the north up to the natural boundaries of the Himalayas and to the east into what is now Assam. To the west, it reached beyond modern Pakistan, to the Hindu Kush mountains in what is now Afghanistan. The empire was established by Chandragupta Maurya in Magadha (in modern Bihar) when he overthrew the Nanda Dynasty. Chandragupta's son Bindusara succeeded to the throne around 297 BC. source: Tennessee was admitted to the Union on June 1, 1796 as the 16th state. It was the first state created from territory under the jurisdiction of the United States federal government. Apart from the former Thirteen Colonies only Vermont and Kentucky predate Tennessee's statehood, and neither was ever a federal territory. The state boundaries, according to the Constitution of the State of Tennessee, Article I, Section 31, stated that the beginning point for identifying the boundary was the extreme height of the Stone Mountain, at the place where the line of Virginia intersects it, and basically ran the extreme heights of mountain chains through the Appalachian Mountains separating North Carolina from Tennessee past the Indian towns of Cowee and Old Chota, thence along the main ridge of the said mountain (Unicoi Mountain) to the southern boundary of the state; all the territory, lands and waters lying west of said line are included in the boundaries and limits of the newly formed state of Tennessee. Part of the provision also stated that the limits and jurisdiction of the state would include future land acquisition, referencing possible land trade with other states, or the acquisition of territory from west of the Mississippi River.

source: In the 7th century, the Frankish merchant Samo, who supported the Slavs fighting their Avar rulers, became the ruler of the first known Slav state in Central Europe, which, however, most probably did not outlive its founder and ruler. Bulgaria was instrumental in the spread of Slavic literacy and Christianity to the rest of the Slavic world.

source: Ann Arbor was founded in 1824 by land speculators John Allen and Elisha Walker Rumsey. On 25 May 1824, the town plat was registered with Wayne County as "Annarbour;" this represents the earliest known use of the town's name. Allen and Rumsey decided to name it for their wives, both named Ann, and for the stands of Bur Oak in the 640 acres (260 ha) of land they purchased for $800 from the federal government at $1.25 per acre. The local Ojibwa named the settlement kaw-goosh-kaw-nick, after the sound of Allen's sawmill.

source: Following al-Farabi's lead, Avicenna initiated a full-fledged inquiry into the question of being, in which he distinguished between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud). He argued that the fact of existence can not be inferred from or accounted for by the essence of existing things, and that form and matter by themselves cannot interact and originate the movement of the universe or the progressive actualization of existing things. Existence must, therefore, be due to an agent-cause that necessitates, imparts, gives, or adds existence to an essence. To do so, the cause must be an existing thing and coexist with its effect.

source: From the 17th through 19th centuries, the merging of folk beliefs about group differences with scientific explanations of those differences produced what one scholar has called an "ideology of race". According to this ideology, races are primordial, natural, enduring and distinct. It was further argued that some groups may be the result of mixture between formerly distinct populations, but that careful study could distinguish the ancestral races that had combined to produce admixed groups. Subsequent influential classifications by Georges Buffon, Petrus Camper and Christoph Meiners all classified "Negros" as inferior to Europeans. In the United States the racial theories of Thomas Jefferson were influential. He saw Africans as inferior to Whites especially in regards to their intellect, and imbued with unnatural sexual appetites, but described Native Americans as equals to whites.

source: Czech distinguishes three genders—masculine, feminine, and neuter—and the masculine gender is subdivided into animate and inanimate. With few exceptions, feminine nouns in the nominative case end in -a, -e, or -ost; neuter nouns in -o, -e, or -í, and masculine nouns in a consonant. Adjectives agree in gender and animacy (for masculine nouns in the accusative or genitive singular and the nominative plural) with the nouns they modify. The main effect of gender in Czech is the difference in noun and adjective declension, but other effects include past-tense verb endings: for example, dělal (he did, or made); dělala (she did, or made) and dělalo (it did, or made).

He suggests that the inclusion of noblewomen in the French "lodges of adoption" during the 1780s was a result of the organization's close ties to the aristocracy rather than a move toward social equality.

source: In response to a given problem situation (), a number of competing conjectures, or tentative theories (), are systematically subjected to the most rigorous attempts at falsification possible. This process, error elimination (), performs a similar function for science that natural selection performs for biological evolution. Theories that better survive the process of refutation are not more true, but rather, more "fit"—in other words, more applicable to the problem situation at hand (). Consequently, just as a species' biological fitness does not ensure continued survival, neither does rigorous testing protect a scientific theory from refutation in the future. Yet, as it appears that the engine of biological evolution has, over many generations, produced adaptive traits equipped to deal with more and more complex problems of survival, likewise, the evolution of theories through the scientific method may, in Popper's view, reflect a certain type of progress: toward more and more interesting problems (). For Popper, it is in the interplay between the tentative theories (conjectures) and error elimination (refutation) that scientific knowledge advances toward greater and greater problems; in a process very much akin to the interplay between genetic variation and natural selection.

source: As the premiers did not come to an agreement on this question, the Parliamentary Council was supposed to address this issue. Its provisions are reflected in Article 29. There was a binding provision for a new delimitation of the federal territory: the Federal Territory must be revised ... (paragraph 1). Moreover, in territories or parts of territories whose affiliation with a Land had changed after 8 May 1945 without a referendum, people were allowed to petition for a revision of the current status within a year after the promulgation of the Basic Law (paragraph 2). If at least one tenth of those entitled to vote in Bundestag elections were in favour of a revision, the federal government had to include the proposal into its legislation. Then a referendum was required in each territory or part of a territory whose affiliation was to be changed (paragraph 3). The proposal should not take effect if within any of the affected territories a majority rejected the change. In this case, the bill had to be introduced again and after passing had to be confirmed by referendum in the Federal Republic as a whole (paragraph 4). The reorganization should be completed within three years after the Basic Law had come into force (paragraph 6).

This article included a binding mandate to revise the delimitation of the federal territory (paragraph 1). Additionally, residents of territories or parts of territories whose affiliation with a Land had changed after May 8, 1945, without a referendum, were permitted to petition for a status revision within one year of the Basic Law's promulgation (paragraph 2). The reorganization was to be finalized within three years of the Basic Law taking effect (paragraph 6).

source: Santa Bárbara became the launching place for expeditions into New Mexico by Spanish conquistadors like: Antonio de Espejo, Gaspar Castaño, Antonio Gutiérrez de Umaña, Francisco Leyba de Bonilla, and Vicente de Zaldívar. Several expeditions were led to find a shorter route from Santa Barbara to New Mexico. In April 1598, Juan de Oñate finally found a short route from Santa Barbara to New Mexico which came to be called El Paso del Norte (The Northern Pass). The discovery of El Paso Del Norte was important for the expansion of El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro (The Inner Land Royal Road) to link Spanish settlements in New Mexico to Mexico City; El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro facilitated transport of settlers and supplies to New Mexico.

source: The entire Protestant canon of scripture is considered the inspired, inerrant word of God. Jehovah's Witnesses consider the Bible to be scientifically and historically accurate and reliable and interpret much of it literally, but accept parts of it as symbolic. They consider the Bible to be the final authority for all their beliefs, although sociologist Andrew Holden's ethnographic study of the religion concluded that pronouncements of the Governing Body, through Watch Tower Society publications, carry almost as much weight as the Bible. Regular personal Bible reading is frequently recommended; Witnesses are discouraged from formulating doctrines and "private ideas" reached through Bible research independent of Watch Tower Society publications, and are cautioned against reading other religious literature. Adherents are told to have "complete confidence" in the leadership, avoid skepticism about what is taught in the Watch Tower Society's literature, and "not advocate or insist on personal opinions or harbor private ideas when it comes to Bible understanding." The religion makes no provision for members to criticize or contribute to official teachings and all Witnesses must abide by its doctrines and organizational requirements.

source: The Laurentian Highlands, the Interior Plains and the Interior Highlands lie between the two coasts, stretching from the Gulf of Mexico northward, far beyond the national boundary, to the Arctic Ocean. The upper Mississippi and some of the Ohio basin is the semi-arid prairie region, with trees originally only along the watercourses. source: Anthropologists have contributed to the debate by shifting the focus of research: One of the first challenges for the researcher wishing to carry out empirical research in this area is to identify an appropriate analytical tool. The concept of boundaries is useful here for demonstrating how identity works. In the same way as Barth, in his approach to ethnicity, advocated the critical focus for investigation as being "the ethnic boundary that defines the group rather than the cultural stuff that it encloses" (1969:15), social anthropologists such as Cohen and Bray have shifted the focus of analytical study from identity to the boundaries that are used for purposes of identification. If identity is a kind of virtual site in which the dynamic processes and markers used for identification are made apparent, boundaries provide the framework on which this virtual site is built. They concentrated on how the idea of community belonging is differently constructed by individual members and how individuals within the group conceive ethnic boundaries.

baseline_output: Anthropologists have shaped the debate by redirecting research toward the mechanisms of identification. A primary challenge for empirical researchers in this field is selecting an appropriate analytical framework, where the concept of "boundaries" serves as a vital tool for understanding identity. Mirroring Fredrik Barth’s assertion that ethnicity is defined by the boundaries between groups rather than the internal cultural content (1969:15), social anthropologists like Cohen and Bray have shifted the analytical focus from identity itself to the boundaries used to establish it. In this view, if identity is a virtual space where the processes of identification become visible, boundaries constitute the underlying framework of that space. Consequently, research has centered on how individual members construct their sense of community belonging and how they perceive the ethnic boundaries that define their group.

source: The key characteristic of classical music that distinguishes it from popular music and folk music is that the repertoire tends to be written down in musical notation, creating a musical part or score. This score typically determines details of rhythm, pitch, and, where two or more musicians (whether singers or instrumentalists) are involved, how the various parts are coordinated. The written quality of the music has enabled a high level of complexity within them: J.S. Bach's fugues, for instance, achieve a remarkable marriage of boldly distinctive melodic lines weaving in counterpoint yet creating a coherent harmonic logic that would be impossible in the heat of live improvisation. The use of written notation also preserves a record of the works and enables Classical musicians to perform music from many centuries ago. Musical notation enables 2000s-era performers to sing a choral work from the 1300s Renaissance era or a 1700s Baroque concerto with many of the features of the music (the melodies, lyrics, forms, and rhythms) being reproduced.

These scores dictate specific details regarding rhythm, pitch, and the coordination of multiple performers. This written format allows for a level of complexity—such as the intricate counterpoint and harmonic logic found in J.S. Bach's fugues—that would be difficult to achieve through live improvisation alone. Furthermore, notation serves as a historical record, allowing modern musicians to accurately reproduce the melodies, lyrics, forms, and rhythms of works spanning centuries, from the 1300s Renaissance to the 1700s Baroque era.

source: The Maurya Empire (322–185 BCE) was the first empire to unify India into one state, and was the largest on the Indian subcontinent. At its greatest extent, the Mauryan Empire stretched to the north up to the natural boundaries of the Himalayas and to the east into what is now Assam. To the west, it reached beyond modern Pakistan, to the Hindu Kush mountains in what is now Afghanistan. The empire was established by Chandragupta Maurya in Magadha (in modern Bihar) when he overthrew the Nanda Dynasty. Chandragupta's son Bindusara succeeded to the throne around 297 BC. By the time he died in c. 272 BC, a large part of the subcontinent was under Mauryan suzerainty. However, the region of Kalinga (around modern day Odisha) remained outside Mauryan control, perhaps interfering with their trade with the south.

source: Tennessee was admitted to the Union on June 1, 1796 as the 16th state. It was the first state created from territory under the jurisdiction of the United States federal government. Apart from the former Thirteen Colonies only Vermont and Kentucky predate Tennessee's statehood, and neither was ever a federal territory. The state boundaries, according to the Constitution of the State of Tennessee, Article I, Section 31, stated that the beginning point for identifying the boundary was the extreme height of the Stone Mountain, at the place where the line of Virginia intersects it, and basically ran the extreme heights of mountain chains through the Appalachian Mountains separating North Carolina from Tennessee past the Indian towns of Cowee and Old Chota, thence along the main ridge of the said mountain (Unicoi Mountain) to the southern boundary of the state; all the territory, lands and waters lying west of said line are included in the boundaries and limits of the newly formed state of Tennessee. Part of the provision also stated that the limits and jurisdiction of the state would include future land acquisition, referencing possible land trade with other states, or the acquisition of territory from west of the Mississippi River.

The line followed the Appalachian mountain chains separating North Carolina and Tennessee, passing the Indian towns of Cowee and Old Chota, and continuing along the main ridge of Unicoi Mountain to the southern border. All lands and waters west of this line were included in the state. Additionally, the provision stipulated that the state's jurisdiction would encompass any future land acquisitions, including potential trades with other states or territories gained west of the Mississippi River.

source: Following al-Farabi's lead, Avicenna initiated a full-fledged inquiry into the question of being, in which he distinguished between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud). He argued that the fact of existence can not be inferred from or accounted for by the essence of existing things, and that form and matter by themselves cannot interact and originate the movement of the universe or the progressive actualization of existing things. Existence must, therefore, be due to an agent-cause that necessitates, imparts, gives, or adds existence to an essence. To do so, the cause must be an existing thing and coexist with its effect.
output: Following the ideas of al-Farabi, Avicenna started a deep study into what it means to "be." He made a distinction between "essence" (what a thing is) and "existence" (the fact that it actually exists). He argued that you cannot figure out why something exists just by looking at what it is. He also believed that "form" and "matter" cannot work together on their own to create movement in the universe or help things grow and change. Therefore, existence must come from an "agent-cause." This cause is what gives or adds existence to an essence. To do this, the cause must be something that already exists and must exist at the same time as the thing it creates.

source: From the 17th through 19th centuries, the merging of folk beliefs about group differences with scientific explanations of those differences produced what one scholar has called an "ideology of race". According to this ideology, races are primordial, natural, enduring and distinct. It was further argued that some groups may be the result of mixture between formerly distinct populations, but that careful study could distinguish the ancestral races that had combined to produce admixed groups. Subsequent influential classifications by Georges Buffon, Petrus Camper and Christoph Meiners all classified "Negros" as inferior to Europeans. In the United States the racial theories of Thomas Jefferson were influential. He saw Africans as inferior to Whites especially in regards to their intellect, and imbued with unnatural sexual appetites, but described Native Americans as equals to whites.
output: Between the 1700s and 1800s, people started mixing old folk beliefs about group differences with new scientific ideas. This created what some experts call an "ideology of race." This idea claimed that different races were natural, permanent, and completely separate from each other. Some people argued that even if groups mixed together, careful study could still show which original races they came from. Famous thinkers like Georges Buffon, Petrus Camper, and Christoph Meiners all wrote that people of African descent were lower than Europeans. In the United States, the ideas of Thomas Jefferson were very important. He believed that Africans were less intelligent than White people and had unnatural desires, but he described Native Americans as being equal to White people.

source: Czech distinguishes three genders—masculine, feminine, and neuter—and the masculine gender is subdivided into animate and inanimate. With few exceptions, feminine nouns in the nominative case end in -a, -e, or -ost; neuter nouns in -o, -e, or -í, and masculine nouns in a consonant. Adjectives agree in gender and animacy (for masculine nouns in the accusative or genitive singular and the nominative plural) with the nouns they modify. The main effect of gender in Czech is the difference in noun and adjective declension, but other effects include past-tense verb endings: for example, dělal (he did, or made); dělala (she did, or made) and dělalo (it did, or made).
output:
Czech has three genders: masculine, feminine, and neuter. The masculine gender is split into two groups: things that are alive (animate) and things that are not alive (inanimate). 

Most feminine nouns end in -a, -e, or -ost. Neuter nouns usually end in -o, -e, or -í. Masculine nouns usually end in a consonant. 

Adjectives must match the gender and animacy of the nouns they describe. This happens in most cases, but specifically in the masculine accusative and genitive singular, and the nominative plural. 

The biggest way gender matters in Czech is how nouns and adjectives change their endings. However, gender also changes the endings of past-tense verbs. For example, the word for "did" or "made" changes based on who did it: dělal (he did), dělala (she did), and dělalo (it did).

Cubism reemerged during the 1920s and the 1930s in the work of the American Stuart Davis and the Englishman Ben Nicholson. In France, however, Cubism experienced a decline beginning in about 1925. source: German historian Reinhart Koselleck claimed that "On the Continent there were two social structures that left a decisive imprint on the Age of Enlightenment: the Republic of Letters and the Masonic lodges." Scottish professor Thomas Munck argues that "although the Masons did promote international and cross-social contacts which were essentially non-religious and broadly in agreement with enlightened values, they can hardly be described as a major radical or reformist network in their own right." Many of the Masons values seemed to greatly appeal to Enlightenment values and thinkers. Diderot discusses the link between Freemason ideals and the enlightenment in D'Alembert's Dream, exploring masonry as a way of spreading enlightenment beliefs. Historian Margaret Jacob stresses the importance of the Masons in indirectly inspiring enlightened political thought. On the negative side, Daniel Roche contests claims that Masonry promoted egalitarianism. He argues that the lodges only attracted men of similar social backgrounds. The presence of noble women in the French "lodges of adoption" that formed in the 1780s was largely due to the close ties shared between these lodges and aristocratic society.

He argues that the lodges mostly attracted men who were already from the same social classes. He also points out that when noble women joined "lodges of adoption" in France during the 1780s, it was mostly because those lodges were very closely connected to the upper class.

source: In response to a given problem situation (), a number of competing conjectures, or tentative theories (), are systematically subjected to the most rigorous attempts at falsification possible. This process, error elimination (), performs a similar function for science that natural selection performs for biological evolution. Theories that better survive the process of refutation are not more true, but rather, more "fit"—in other words, more applicable to the problem situation at hand (). Consequently, just as a species' biological fitness does not ensure continued survival, neither does rigorous testing protect a scientific theory from refutation in the future. Yet, as it appears that the engine of biological evolution has, over many generations, produced adaptive traits equipped to deal with more and more complex problems of survival, likewise, the evolution of theories through the scientific method may, in Popper's view, reflect a certain type of progress: toward more and more interesting problems (). For Popper, it is in the interplay between the tentative theories (conjectures) and error elimination (refutation) that scientific knowledge advances toward greater and greater problems; in a process very much akin to the interplay between genetic variation and natural selection.
output:
When scientists face a problem, they come up with many different guesses or ideas. They then try very hard to prove those ideas wrong. This process of finding and removing mistakes is called "error elimination." It works for science in a way that is very similar to how natural selection works in nature.

The theories that survive these tests are not necessarily "more true." Instead, they are more "fit," which means they work better for the specific problem being studied. Just as being fit doesn't mean an animal will live forever, passing a test doesn't mean a scientific theory will never be proven wrong in the future.

However, just as natural selection helps animals develop traits to handle harder survival problems over time, the scientific method helps theories improve. According to a thinker named Popper, this shows a type of progress: science moves toward solving more and more interesting problems. For Popper, scientific knowledge grows because of the interaction between new guesses and the process of finding errors. This is very much like how the mix of genetic variety and natural selection helps life evolve.

source: As the premiers did not come to an agreement on this question, the Parliamentary Council was supposed to address this issue. Its provisions are reflected in Article 29. There was a binding provision for a new delimitation of the federal territory: the Federal Territory must be revised ... (paragraph 1). Moreover, in territories or parts of territories whose affiliation with a Land had changed after 8 May 1945 without a referendum, people were allowed to petition for a revision of the current status within a year after the promulgation of the Basic Law (paragraph 2). If at least one tenth of those entitled to vote in Bundestag elections were in favour of a revision, the federal government had to include the proposal into its legislation. Then a referendum was required in each territory or part of a territory whose affiliation was to be changed (paragraph 3). The proposal should not take effect if within any of the affected territories a majority rejected the change. In this case, the bill had to be introduced again and after passing had to be confirmed by referendum in the Federal Republic as a whole (paragraph 4). The reorganization should be completed within three years after the Basic Law had come into force (paragraph 6).

source: Anthropologists have contributed to the debate by shifting the focus of research: One of the first challenges for the researcher wishing to carry out empirical research in this area is to identify an appropriate analytical tool. The concept of boundaries is useful here for demonstrating how identity works. In the same way as Barth, in his approach to ethnicity, advocated the critical focus for investigation as being "the ethnic boundary that defines the group rather than the cultural stuff that it encloses" (1969:15), social anthropologists such as Cohen and Bray have shifted the focus of analytical study from identity to the boundaries that are used for purposes of identification. If identity is a kind of virtual site in which the dynamic processes and markers used for identification are made apparent, boundaries provide the framework on which this virtual site is built. They concentrated on how the idea of community belonging is differently constructed by individual members and how individuals within the group conceive ethnic boundaries.
output: Anthropologists have helped this debate by changing what researchers look at. When someone wants to study this topic, one of the first things they must do is find the right tool to use for their study. The idea of "boundaries" is a helpful tool for showing how identity works. Just like a researcher named Barth, who said we should study the "ethnic boundary" that defines a group instead of just the culture inside it, other experts like Cohen and Bray changed the focus. Instead of just looking at identity, they looked at the boundaries people use to identify who they are. If identity is like a space where the signs of belonging are shown, then boundaries are the frame that builds that space. These researchers focused on how different people in a group think about belonging and how they imagine the lines that separate their group from others.

baseline_output: Anthropologists have shaped the debate by redirecting research toward the mechanisms of identification. A primary challenge for empirical researchers in this field is selecting an appropriate analytical framework, where the concept of "boundaries" serves as a vital tool for understanding identity. Mirroring Fredrik Barth’s assertion that ethnicity is defined by the boundaries between groups rather than the internal cultural content (1969:15), social anthropologists like Cohen and Bray have shifted the analytical focus from identity itself to the boundaries used to establish it. In this view, if identity is a virtual space where the processes of identification become visible, boundaries constitute the underlying framework of that space. Consequently, research has centered on how individual members construct their sense of community belonging and how they perceive the ethnic boundaries that define their group.

source: The key characteristic of classical music that distinguishes it from popular music and folk music is that the repertoire tends to be written down in musical notation, creating a musical part or score. This score typically determines details of rhythm, pitch, and, where two or more musicians (whether singers or instrumentalists) are involved, how the various parts are coordinated. The written quality of the music has enabled a high level of complexity within them: J.S. Bach's fugues, for instance, achieve a remarkable marriage of boldly distinctive melodic lines weaving in counterpoint yet creating a coherent harmonic logic that would be impossible in the heat of live improvisation. The use of written notation also preserves a record of the works and enables Classical musicians to perform music from many centuries ago. Musical notation enables 2000s-era performers to sing a choral work from the 1300s Renaissance era or a 1700s Baroque concerto with many of the features of the music (the melodies, lyrics, forms, and rhythms) being reproduced.
output:
The main thing that makes classical music different from popular or folk music is that it is usually written down in musical notes. This written music is called a score. The score tells the musicians exactly which notes to play, what the rhythm is, and how everyone should work together at the same time.

Because the music is written down, it can be very complicated. For example, the music of J.S. Bach has many different melodies playing at once that fit together perfectly. This would be too hard for musicians to make up on the spot while they are performing.

Writing music down also helps keep it safe for the future. It allows musicians today to play music that was written hundreds of years ago. Because of these notes, a singer today can perform a song from the 1300s or a piece from the 1700s and still keep the same melodies, words, shapes, and rhythms as the original.

source: The Maurya Empire (322–185 BCE) was the first empire to unify India into one state, and was the largest on the Indian subcontinent. At its greatest extent, the Mauryan Empire stretched to the north up to the natural boundaries of the Himalayas and to the east into what is now Assam. To the west, it reached beyond modern Pakistan, to the Hindu Kush mountains in what is now Afghanistan. The empire was established by Chandragupta Maurya in Magadha (in modern Bihar) when he overthrew the Nanda Dynasty. Chandragupta's son Bindusara succeeded to the throne around 297 BC. By the time he died in c. 272 BC, a large part of the subcontinent was under Mauryan suzerainty. However, the region of Kalinga (around modern day Odisha) remained outside Mauryan control, perhaps interfering with their trade with the south.

Despite this vast expansion, the region of Kalinga (near modern Odisha) remained independent, potentially obstructing Mauryan trade routes to the south.

Apart from the former Thirteen Colonies only Vermont and Kentucky predate Tennessee's statehood, and neither was ever a federal territory. The state boundaries, according to the Constitution of the State of Tennessee, Article I, Section 31, stated that the beginning point for identifying the boundary was the extreme height of the Stone Mountain, at the place where the line of Virginia intersects it, and basically ran the extreme heights of mountain chains through the Appalachian Mountains separating North Carolina from Tennessee past the Indian towns of Cowee and Old Chota, thence along the main ridge of the said mountain (Unicoi Mountain) to the southern boundary of the state; all the territory, lands and waters lying west of said line are included in the boundaries and limits of the newly formed state of Tennessee. Part of the provision also stated that the limits and jurisdiction of the state would include future land acquisition, referencing possible land trade with other states, or the acquisition of territory from west of the Mississippi River.
